Rising electricity demand, especially from AI and data centers, has brought nuclear and geothermal back into focus as sources of clean, firm power. But demand, corporate partnerships and policy support are not the same as projects delivering affordable electricity on time. The central question is whether both technologies can turn renewed momentum into repeatable deployment.
Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie, is joined by Jenifer Shafer, professor of chemistry and Ben L. Fryrear Presidential Chair at Colorado School of Mines, and Anna Littlefield, Geothermal and Low Carbon Technologies Program Manager at the Payne Institute for Public Policy. They compare what is driving this moment and where the routes to scale diverge. On nuclear, uprates and restarts could add capacity sooner than new builds, while small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s. Shafer explains how fuel recycling could improve fuel security and reduce the amount of material requiring disposal, but would not remove the need for a repository. Cost, safeguards and social license remain central challenges, while progress through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch.
Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat in deep rock beyond the limited areas served by conventional hydrothermal resources. Drilling and reservoir engineering have advanced, but the test now is whether projects can sustain heat flow economically over time while managing water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance. Littlefield points to power purchase agreements scheduled for the 2028 to 2030 period as an important test of delivery, not yet proof of scale. Colorado’s permitting and development efforts, including work to assess whether treated oil and gas produced water can support geothermal circulation, may offer lessons for other states.
The technologies face different constraints: nuclear must address fuel, waste and project execution, while geothermal must prove durable reservoirs and manage water and induced-seismicity concerns. Both also depend on community trust. The guests argue that developers need to listen to local concerns and share monitoring data, rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support. Over the next five years, the clearest evidence will be projects that reach operation and perform as promised, alongside nuclear licensing progress and geothermal’s ability to deliver contracted power reliably.
